lessons.title: Array Basics
lessons.concept: An array stores values in contiguous memory locations for fast direct index access. Access is O(1); search/insert/delete are O(n) unless at the end.
lessons.worked_example: arr = [10, 20, 30]. arr[1] = 20 in O(1). Insert at index 0 requires shifting all elements → O(n).
mistakes: Confusing array access O(1) with search O(n)
Forgetting arrays are fixed-size in many languages

lessons.title: Array Traversal
lessons.concept: Visit each element once using a loop. Time O(n), space O(1). Use for finding max, sum, search.
lessons.worked_example: Find max: initialize max = arr[0]; loop i=1..n-1; if arr[i] > max, max = arr[i].

practice.question: Time complexity of accessing an element in an array?
practice.explanation: Arrays support direct index access → O(1).

practice.question: Which is NOT a linear data structure?
practice.explanation: Tree is non-linear (hierarchical). Array, linked list, queue are linear.

practice.question: In a 0-indexed array of length n, the last element is at index:
practice.explanation: 0-based indexing runs 0..n-1, so the final element is at n - 1 (using n causes an out-of-bounds error).

practice.question: Average time to access an array element by index is:
practice.explanation: Arrays provide random access: the address is computed directly (base + index * size), giving constant-time access.

practice.question: Which of these is NOT a typical array operation?
practice.explanation: Inserting at the front shifts every element: O(n), not O(1). Index access, traversal and in-place reverse (two-pointer swap) are standard.

practice.question: In column-major storage of an R x C matrix, elements of the same _____ are contiguous.
practice.explanation: Column-major lays out each column's elements adjacently (Fortran/MATLAB style); row-major is the C/C++ default.

practice.question: Rotating an array right by k positions optimally runs in:

options.A: O(n) with O(1) extra space using reversals
options.C: O(1) by changing only the index base

practice.explanation: Reverse-all, then reverse first k, then reverse the rest: three O(n) passes in O(1) space (or use an O(k) extra array).

questions.question: What does this do for array arr of size n? for(i=0;i<n;i++) arr[i]=i;
questions.explanation: Each element arr[i] is set to its own index i.

questions.question: Best for implementing back functionality in a web browser?
questions.explanation: Back uses LIFO (last visited page first) → stack.

questions.question: Stable sorting algorithm?
questions.explanation: Merge sort is stable (preserves relative order of equal elements).

questions.question: Which operation is typically O(n) on an array (shifting elements)?
questions.explanation: Insertion at position 0 shifts all n elements right: O(n). Index reads/updates are O(1); end append is O(1) amortised; deletion at an index also shifts (O(n)).

questions.question: To traverse an array once and print each element, the loop runs how many iterations?
questions.explanation: A full forward traversal visits every one of the n elements exactly once: n iterations (0 to n-1 inclusive).

questions.question: Reverse an array of length n in place with optimal time complexity. Best achievable =
questions.explanation: Swap element i with element n-1-i for i < n/2: n/2 swaps = O(n) time, O(1) extra space (every element must move at least once, so O(n) is optimal).

questions.question: Two-sum on an UNSORTED array can be solved in O(n) using:

options.B: A hash set of seen values

questions.explanation: As you scan, check whether (target - x) was already seen; if not, store x. Sorting would also give O(n log n), not pure O(n).

questions.question: What is the best-case complexity of checking whether an array is sorted?

options.A: O(1) only if you trust metadata
options.B: O(n) - every adjacent pair may need comparison

questions.explanation: You must verify all n-1 adjacent pairs (an early exit gives best case O(n) early, but still linear in the checked prefix); no sublinear method can certify sortedness of arbitrary data.
